sections.title: Name and identification
sections.text: Species Fungorum accepts Clitocybe nebularis (Batsch) P. Kumm.; Lepista nebularis is a taxonomic synonym. The clouded funnel forms large ash-grey to grey-brown caps, sometimes covered by a whitish bloom, especially when young. The cap begins convex, then flattens or becomes slightly depressed; its margin remains inrolled for a long time.

sections.title: Gills, stem and flesh
sections.text: The gills are very crowded, whitish to cream and sometimes slightly yellowish at maturity; they are adnate at first, then slightly to distinctly decurrent, and often forked. The stout whitish to greyish stem often widens toward the base, which may be bulbous and bear white mycelium. The flesh is thick and white. The odor is strong and variable, often unpleasant and farinaceous-rancid, though it may be milder in some collections. The spore print is pale buff to yellowish.

sections.title: Habitat and season
sections.text: This saprotrophic species grows on the ground in leaf litter beneath broadleaf or conifer trees, often in groups or arcs and rings. It fruits mainly in autumn, sometimes late in the season. Size and color vary considerably with age and conditions.

sections.title: Lookalikes and toxicology
sections.text: The Belgian Poison Centre warns of possible confusion with the livid pinkgill (Entoloma sinuatum). Its gills are typically notched and its spore print turns pink at maturity, whereas C. nebularis has pale, decurrent gills; these features alone are not enough to identify a specimen. VAPKO now classifies C. nebularis as inedible. Japan’s Ministry of Health reports gastrointestinal poisonings but says the responsible toxic principle remains uncertain. Nebularine has been detected and motivates a precautionary long-term concern, although mutagenicity has not been demonstrated in humans.

traits: Large cap, 5–25 cm, ash-grey to grey-brown, often whitish-pruinose when young; convex then flat to slightly depressed, margin long inrolled
Very crowded, whitish to cream gills, sometimes yellowing, adnate then decurrent and often forked
Stout, whitish to greyish stem, often widened or bulbous at the base, sometimes covered in white mycelium
Thick white flesh; odor strong and often unpleasant, farinaceous or rancid, but variable
Pale buff to yellowish spore print
On the ground in leaf litter under broadleaf or conifer trees, often in groups or rings, mainly in autumn
safetyNote: Do not eat Clitocybe nebularis: VAPKO classifies it as inedible, and Japan’s Ministry of Health advises against eating it. Vomiting, abdominal pain and diarrhea have been reported; the principle responsible for acute symptoms has not been established. Nebularine has been detected, and VAPKO advises against consumption as a precaution, but the sources do not demonstrate cancer or mutation risk in humans. Confusion with the poisonous livid pinkgill is also reported. If ingested, contact poison control or emergency services promptly.
